sections.title: Core Foundations & Conceptual Framework
sections.content:
• **Defence of India Act (1915)**: Enacted as a wartime emergency measure to curtail civil liberties, it granted the government sweeping powers to censor the press and suppress 'seditious' literature.
• **Wartime Censorship**: The colonial state utilized the **Press Act of 1910** to demand heavy security deposits from nationalist newspapers, effectively silencing dissent during the war years.
• **Post-War Radicalization**: The **Rowlatt Act (1919)** and the Jallianwala Bagh massacre triggered a surge in nationalist journalism, leading to the rise of papers like 'Young India' and 'Navjivan'.
• **Key Metric**: The shift from 'moderate' critique to 'mass-mobilization' rhetoric defined the post-1919 press landscape.

sections.title: Comprehensive Classification & Comparative Matrix
rows: Strict censorship, focus on war effort, suppression of Home Rule League views.
Defence of India Act (1915) & Press Act (1910).
Prelims: Focus on legislative tools used for suppression.
Aggressive nationalist tone, focus on Khilafat and Non-Cooperation.
Repeal of Press Act (1922) following Tej Bahadur Sapru Committee.
Mains: Role of press in mass mobilization.

items.definition: Empowered magistrates to demand security from printers/publishers; if 'seditious' content was found, security was forfeited and the press confiscated.
Appointed to review the Press Acts; its recommendations led to the repeal of the 1910 Act in 1922, a rare instance of colonial concession.

items.title: Major Applications / Initiatives
items.content:
• **Gandhian Journalism**: Use of 'Young India' and 'Navjivan' to propagate Satyagraha and Swadeshi.
• **Home Rule Press**: Tilak's 'Maratha' and 'Kesari' and Annie Besant's 'New India' served as the primary vehicles for political education.

items.title: Challenges & Way Forward
items.content:
• **Key Challenges**: Financial bankruptcy due to security forfeitures and imprisonment of editors.
• **Solutions**: Shift to underground pamphlets and clandestine printing presses during the peak of the Non-Cooperation Movement.

items.title: Mnemonic for Retention
items.content:
• **Memory Acronym**: 'D-R-S' (Defence, Rowlatt, Sapru).
• **Decoded Meaning**: D (Defence of India Act 1915) -> R (Rowlatt Act 1919) -> S (Sapru Committee 1921/Repeal 1922).

upscNotes.content: Examiner Trap: UPSC often confuses the 'Press Act of 1910' with the 'Vernacular Press Act of 1878'. Remember: 1910 Act applied to ALL presses, not just vernacular.
Mains Value Addition: Use the term 'Democratic Deficit' to describe the colonial press policy during the war, contrasting it with the 'Fourth Estate' role of the nationalist press.

keyTakeaways: The Defence of India Act (1915) was the primary tool for wartime press suppression.
The 1910 Press Act was repealed in 1922 based on the recommendations of the Sapru Committee.
Post-WWI journalism shifted from elite intellectual discourse to mass-based political agitation.
